sections.title: Search for life, not just deep water
sections.text:
An empty-looking ocean becomes easier to read when you look for food. Watch for birds working one area, bait near the surface, or fish breaking beside floating cover. A current edge or a weed line deserves a careful pass when it also shows life. Floating Sargassum supports young fish and other animals, which helps explain its value in an offshore search.

Use local seasonal reports to choose the target and trip date. Start in daylight when you first learn to spot birds, bait, and current edges. Mahi mahi around floating cover call for a different approach from tuna holding deep or grouper beside a wreck. Use the sounder and the crew’s recent knowledge to choose the working depth. Mark a bite or visible school so you can return to the same water. Approach a feeding group from the edge. Driving through its middle scatters the opportunity and can spoil the fishing for other boats.

sections.title: Make the trolling spread work
sections.text:
Before the boat reaches the fishing area, learn which rod is yours and how its drag works. For trolling, the crew sets lures or baits at different distances so they run cleanly behind the boat. Watch each one near the surface before it goes farther back. A bait that spins or a lure packed with weed needs attention, even if the rest of the spread looks good.

When a fish strikes, follow the crew’s call. Keep steady pressure and wind when you can gain line. Avoid pumping the rod so high that you lose control near the tip. Other anglers should clear spare lines and loose gear. Ask for help before a fish crosses the stern or heads beneath the boat. Let the crew handle heavy leaders. A strong run can tighten a loose loop dangerously fast.

sections.title: Be ready to cast or drop
sections.text:
A school beside floating cover may give you a chance to cast. Keep a suitable spinning rod ready with a baitfish lure or jig, and leave the hook secured until the skipper positions the boat. Cast clear of other lines and retrieve through the edge of the school. If fish follow without taking, change the speed or let the lure sink a little deeper.

For fish marked below the boat, lower a jig to the indicated depth and work that layer. You do not need to touch bottom when the fish sit above it. Count the drop or use marked line so you can repeat the depth after a bite. Carry only tackle that fits the target and the crew’s method. A heavy jigging outfit and a light casting outfit have different jobs, even on the same trip.

sections.title: Prepare for the whole day at sea
sections.text:
Choose an experienced crew for a first offshore trip. Ask about the target, method, travel time, and equipment before departure. Check the marine forecast and accept a shorter route or cancellation when conditions demand it. Pack drinking water, sun cover, rain protection, and shoes that grip a wet deck. Keep personal items in one compact bag away from the work area.

Listen to the safety briefing and locate the life jackets and emergency equipment. Know where to stand during a strike and where to move when a large fish reaches the boat. Never wrap a leader around your hand or brace against an unsecured rod. Keep hooks covered during travel. Respect another boat’s drift or trolling path. For released fish, let the crew unhook them with minimal handling and keep large fish in the water whenever possible.

checklist: Leave heavy leaders to the crew.

evidence.claim: Floating Sargassum provides nursery habitat for mahi mahi, jacks and amberjacks.
Offshore methods include trolling, jigging and bottom fishing, with different tackle for different targets; beginners benefit from a charter or guide.
Tackle that lands fish promptly and dehooking with minimal air exposure support successful release.
FWC identifies floating debris, Sargassum, current edges, eddies and water-color changes as places to look for offshore fish.

habitats.name: Kayak fishing
habitats.title: Kayak Fishing: Get Close and Keep the Boat Simple
habitats.summary: Use a kayak to reach lake edges, sheltered bays, and gentle rivers. Set up a clean deck, control your drift, and land fish from a seat.

sections.title: Choose water that fits your paddling skills
sections.text:
Start on a small, sheltered lake or protected bay with an easy launch and landing. Learn to paddle, turn, stop, and recover from a capsize before you add fishing gear. Practice rescue skills with qualified help in controlled conditions. A wide fishing kayak still needs a skilled paddler when wind, current, or waves increase. Leave exposed coasts and strong rivers for suitable training and equipment.

Choose one short route with several nearby fishing stops. Check the wind, weather, water temperature, and tide where relevant. An easy outward drift can become a hard paddle home. Leave a float plan with someone ashore and carry a reliable way to call for help. Wear a properly fitted life jacket throughout the trip. Dress for an unexpected immersion, including appropriate cold-water protection when the water demands it.

sections.title: Rig the boat so everything has a place
sections.text:
Begin with one rod and a small tackle box. Put pliers, spare leader, and a compact net where you can reach them without twisting far behind the seat. Secure the box and loose items. Keep hooks covered until you need them. Arrange the paddle so you can take hold of it immediately, even with a fish on. Avoid loose cords and loops around your legs.

Choose tackle for the water, just as you would from shore. A weedless plastic suits a lake edge; a light jig or shrimp imitation can suit a sheltered saltwater flat. Practice short casts while seated before the trip. Check that the lure clears rods and equipment behind you. Pack drinking water and weather layers within reach. Leave unnecessary spare gear ashore so the working area stays clear when a fish arrives.

sections.title: Set the drift before you cast
sections.text:
Stop short of the cover and see how the boat moves. A small amount of wind or current can carry you past a useful edge while you cast ahead. Make a short pass, then paddle back outside the fishing area to repeat it. Keep the boat away from the bank you plan to fish. Quiet movement is useful only if you do not drift over the fish first.

In a lake, work along weeds or a point with a jig, small swimbait, or soft plastic. In a sheltered bay, use the same controlled drift beside a grass edge. On a gentle river, plan the next safe stopping point before the cast. Do not anchor in current without suitable equipment and training. Keep clear of submerged branches, dams, navigation channels, and motorboats. Put the rod down whenever boat control needs both hands.

sections.title: Land the fish from the seat
sections.text:
Keep your weight centered and guide the fish alongside the kayak. Leave enough line beyond the rod tip to bring it to the net without pulling the rod straight overhead. Lower the net into the water and guide the fish over it. Avoid a long sideways reach. If the fish surges, let the drag work and settle it again before another attempt.

Keep the hook and fish away from your legs. Use pliers and support the fish for a quick release beside the boat. A photograph can wait if the kayak drifts toward trouble. Give bank anglers and other paddlers space, and keep your wake small near wildlife. Return while you still have energy and daylight. At the launch, unload away from the ramp, then drain and clean the kayak before it goes to another water.

checklist: Land fish with your weight centered.

evidence.claim: FWC advises paddlers to wear flotation, check tides and wind, leave a float plan, carry communications and give anglers room.
Cold-water immersion can impair breathing and movement; flotation and clothing matched to water temperature improve preparedness.
Take Me Fishing advises leaving enough line beyond the rod tip when landing a fish from a kayak.
